ARC: The Final Stand (661–668)

=== EPISODE 78: Pyongyang I (661)
Red Sun's capital sits on its ridge. A red two-storey gate, grey stone, and clouds that always look about to pick a side. There is only one gate anyone remembers.
The impenetrable walls of Pyongyang are tested once again.
namgun: Pyongyang does not fall. / Not since the Holy King strung his bow. Seven hundred years.
In Luoyang the Third Emperor announces that he will lead the next army himself. The Empress sends up a memorial the same night.
wuzetian: Your father went in person, Majesty. / Ask the six horses at Zhaoling how that went.
gaozong: …We will send someone.
The someone is the Red Fowl. He comes up the Taedong in the eighth month, takes the river forts one by one, and sits down in front of Pyongyang to wait for winter to soften it. Winter has never been on anybody’s side but Goguryeo’s.
In the ninth month, Namseng holds the great river with tens of thousands. It freezes overnight. At dawn the White Dragon walks his army across the ice, drums going. He kills thirty thousand men guarding a river that is no longer there.
gesomun: One river, Namseng. I gave you one river. / Don’t tell me you didn’t know it would freeze. It freezes every year.
The Red Fowl’s army freezes in the snow outside the walls, eats its horses, and waits for rice.
In the twelfth month, a letter comes down from the north. The Red Fowl is out of rice. Munmu reads it to his generals. Nobody offers. Everyone knows that road in winter. Kim Yushin, who is sixty-six, offers.
munmu: Uncle. Not you. Send someone younger.
yushin: The younger ones don’t know the road, Majesty. Hanseul and I do. / Load the carts.
The White Tiger has thirteen sons. Yeon Gesomun can count to thirteen…!

=== EPISODE 79: Snake River (662)
The White Tiger drives his host into the Snake River. They still believe rivers are roads. Yeon Gesomun has been waiting for a man who thinks that. Old men in the north remember another river that ate an army. The Snake is younger. It's hungrier. And it has Yeon's teeth.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 22, Goguryeo Annals — King Bojang, yr. 21 (662); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1 · cf. Zizhi Tongjian Tang Longshuo 2] [The White Tiger] fought Yeon Gaesomun on the Snake River; the whole army was lost, and he and his thirteen sons all died in battle.
## Thirteen Sons
The river does not take them in a heap. Yeon counts. Chang’an’s clerks will later write thirteen sons as if a number were a grave. It is a morning. The water is February-cold and already learning names.
The thirteenth and the twelfth come together at the first bend — brothers who still share a horse’s width. Yeon meets them in the shallows where the current lies. One stroke. Two bodies. The horse walks on a few steps with no one left to tell it to stop.
gesomun: Thirteen. / Twelve.
The eleventh tries the reeds. Reeds keep a secret until a man breathes too loud. Yeon does not spend a speech on a boy hiding in grass.
gesomun: Eleven.
The tenth and the ninth have turned back toward their father. That is the expensive choice: love draws a straight line, and Yeon has been cutting straight lines since the banquet taught him how a room empties. They die reaching for a sleeve that is still too far upriver.
gesomun: Ten. / Nine.
The eighth is the archer. He puts three shafts into the rim of Yeon’s shield and a fourth into the air where Yeon was. He does not finish the fifth. Yeon takes the bow out of the water afterward and breaks it across his knee, because a river should not keep a weapon that almost learned his height.
gesomun: Eight. The bow ends here.
The seventh almost makes the far bank. Almost is the dearest word a river sells. Yeon’s throw finds him between the shoulder-blades; the current finishes the courtesy of carrying him the rest of the way.
the seventh: Baekju… / Home…
gesomun: Seven. Home is not that bank.
Three at once in a knot of horses — the sixth, the fifth, the fourth — the way a man takes a cluster when the line has already broken. They shout one father’s name in three pitches. The Snake does not sort pitches.
gesomun: Six. Five. Four. / Some days you count in threes.
The third is old enough to bargain. He offers the banner, the Lingnan levy, a road south, if the Magreji will count him as a messenger instead of a son.
the third: Let me go as a messenger. / Among the thirteen I am the only one who opened his mouth.
gesomun: You did not come as a messenger. / That is why you are three.
The second is younger. He still wears a name-tab the southern clerks wrote and never expected to read at this latitude. He does not speak. Yeon does not ask him to. The river takes the tab first; the boy follows it as if following orders.
gesomun: Two.
The first — the eldest — holds the White Tiger banner with both hands so the silk will not touch the water. He lasts longer than the others because he has decided to be a flagpole. Yeon cuts the pole. The cloth goes under. The boy goes with it, still holding on, which is how eldest sons are trained.
gesomun: One. / Now the tiger.
## The White Tiger
Then only the tiger is left. The White Tiger of Baekju — White Prefecture, a white that is a hometown and not this river — stands where the Lingnan boys can still see him if any of them still have eyes. Someone shouts to break east, toward any camp that is not this one.
aide: Commander! Toward You Boying’s camp— / Live, and leave the account!
pangxiaotai: I have eaten too much favour under two emperors. / I will not go home while this kingdom still stands. / The southern boys I brought are already dead — / what would this one body do, alive?
He does not run. The arrows make a hedgehog of him — the phrase southern records prefer when they cannot bear to write that he was outfought. Yeon walks the last three steps through water that is no longer sure whether it is a river or a grave, and finishes what the shafts began.
gesomun: White Tiger. / Titles drown too.
gesomun: Still haven’t come to your senses, you bastards?! / I am… none other than… Yeon Gesomun!!
The courier finds Xue Rengui a thousand miles the other way. He has just ended a war in the far west with three arrows. His soldiers are already singing about it. He is given the dead man's title, White Tiger II. And the bill.
xuerengui: White Tiger… I will take the name. / The dead man’s account is paid by the living.
He says it without triumph. The White Tiger’s thirteen sons are still a silence in the Tang camp; Xue Rengui’s job is to make sure that silence does not become the empire’s last word on the east.
The fangtian ji goes east again. Men who never learned his birth name learn the white coat and the crescent blade — and begin, quietly, to fear the second tiger more than the first.
## Yumla Defied
In the worst hour of the fighting — arrows spent, horse down, a Tang blade a finger from his throat — the air thins the way Tamla stories promised. Kangrim and Haewonmek are there. Ledger half-open between them.
kangrim: Yeon Gesomun. / Your page is… persuasive today.
kangrim: Commander. If you walk away now — / are you choosing Goguryeo, or choosing not to be finished by anyone else’s schedule?
haewonmek: Any last words? / Say them now. The blade is already practicing your name.
gesomun: Kangrim. Haewonmek. / Both. / And neither is your business until I am done.
gesomun: Not today. / I still have sons to disappoint.
The soul leaves the body the way a red coat leaves a peg — still his face, still his will. He cuts the escorts in the thinning air, ledger and last-words both, then finds the ice again. Eyes go from dead to locked. The Tang soldier is still in the middle of the stab when the wrist stops.
He stands up on will alone. The blade misses. Both reapers close the ledger with something like respect — the rare expression of His Majesty’s escorts impressed by rudeness. They fail, together, at the Snake River.
kangrim: Hah. / Keep the country a little longer, then. / I hate refiling — and Your Majesty hates wasted parchment.
haewonmek: Next time we bring a longer chain. / Or a taller boss.
## The Rice Road
In the second month a train of carts comes up out of the south through snow to the axles. Kim Yushin is sixty-seven, and he has walked half the road beside his white horse so that Hanseul can carry a sack of rice instead of him.
The Tang camp outside Pyongyang has been eating its horses. Men sit hugging their knees in the snow and look at the carts as if they might be another rumour.
sudingfang: Silla is late. / …Unload it. All of it. Then we go home.
yushin: We came through snow to the horse’s chest, General. / You may eat it slowly.
The Red Fowl takes the rice, breaks camp within the week, and sails. The road back is Yushin’s problem. Goguryeo’s horsemen follow the empty carts all the way to the Imjin, and the white horse carries him across it.
And on an island far to the south, someone is asking: whose side are we on now?

=== EPISODE 80: Tamla Surrenders (662)
After the Snake River, Tamla quietly changes sides.
The island kingdom sends its envoys to Silla and the Tang, ending seven centuries beside Baekje.
Baekje is supposed to be finished. Nobody told the fortresses. And in Surabol, a great lord calls in sick…!

=== EPISODE 81: Rebellion (662)
## Naesaji
Two summers after Sabi, Baekje is supposed to be finished. Nobody has told the fortresses. The leftovers gather at a hill fort east of the old capital. They do what a kingdom does with no king nearby. They collect grain. They hang collaborators. They send boys to watch the Silla roads.
Munmu names nineteen generals for it. One of them is Kim Jinju. He is True Bone, from a good family. He led men at the Yellow Mountain. He has a son in the emperor's guard.
Jinju sends word that he is ill. So does Jinheum, governor of Namcheon. Neither of them is ill. They stay at home through the whole of the campaign, eat well, receive visitors, and are seen at a gyuku match.
Kim Jinju: Nineteen generals for one hill fort. They don’t need a twentieth. / Besides. The war’s over. Somebody should say so.
Naesaji falls without him. Kim Heumsun takes it in a fortnight and reports it to the king in two lines, and then, because he is honest and it is his duty, he reports who was missing.
munmu: Ill. / The whole campaign. Both of them. And well enough for gyuku.
Kim Jinju: Majesty, the fever came and went. A man cannot choose his days—
munmu: My father never had a day off from this war. My sister didn’t get to choose hers. / Take them out.
Jinju and Jinheum are beheaded, and their households with them, down to the cousins. It is the first time Munmu kills his own nobility, barely a year into the reign, and after it nobody mistakes the new king for a soft one.
The annals aren't done with him. Eight years later, the same pages send a Jinju to behead a traitor governor. Later tellers like that version better. They even give him the credit for this hill fort. Either Silla had two men of the name, or a clerk killed him once and forgot. Only one person never mixes them up: his son.
Kim Punghun is at Chang’an when the news comes, in the emperor’s guard, where the sons of vassal houses are kept. He hears it from a Tang officer who is sorry for him, which is worse. He asks for leave to go home for the mourning and is told, kindly, that he has no home to go to.
kimpunghun: …Then I will wait. / The emperor’s ships go east sooner or later. I can wait for a ship.
Back at Juryu, a monk and a general share one army. We have to go back to see who keeps it…!

=== EPISODE 82: Betrayal (661) [flashback]
## Dochim
Before Boksin and the king, there were Boksin and the monk. Dochim raised the first banner with him, the autumn Sabi fell. He put down his begging bowl for a spear. He named himself General of the Spirit Army. For a year the two held the west between them. The enemy garrison couldn't even go out for water.
Then a Tang envoy came to the walls with a letter, and Dochim sent him back with it unread and a message that the General of the Spirit Army did not receive men of so small a rank. It was a good line. Boksin heard it and understood that the monk had begun to think of himself as the one in charge.
dochim: The Buddha gave me this army, Boksin. You only fed it. / Feed it well. It is going to Sabi.
boksin: Of course, General. Whatever the Spirit Army needs. / Supper tonight, then. Just the two of us. We’ll talk about Sabi.
Dochim comes to supper. He does not leave it. By morning his men have been folded into Boksin’s army without a vote, and Prince Pung, newly crowned and still learning the names, is told that the monk has gone on a long retreat.
pung: A retreat. In the middle of a war. / …I see. And who commands his men now?
boksin: I do, Majesty. So that Your Majesty need never worry about it.
Pung remembers the answer. He has two years to think about it.
## The Jar
boksin: In the end it is I who raise this country twice. / And it is he who wears the crown.
boksin: …And he will want to move again.
Boksin plots to kill the king by pretending to be sick, but is caught and executed instead.
Two summers later, in the sixth month of 663, King Pungjang has the general who crowned him bound with a leather thong through the palms, and asks the room whether a man like that should be cut down. The room says yes, Jipdeuk first. Boksin spits at him.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), sixth month] Boksin at once spat at Jipdeuk and said: “Rotten dog, idiot slave!” The king ordered his strong men to behead him, and had the head pickled.
Two generals stand at the back while the head is salted. Heukchi Sangji, who took two hundred fortresses back for Boksin in a single season, watches the king’s hands. Satek Sangya watches the jar.
sangji: The man who crowned him. In a jar. / …What do you think he does with the ones who didn’t?
sateksangya: Same thing. Less salt.
However, there is still a problem. Boksin was the most competent general of the movement, and there is only one chance left.
Four banners. One river mouth. The West, Samhan and the East meet on a single tide…!

=== EPISODE 83: White River (663)
Chang’an’s clerks still count to thirteen when they hear the word river. This mouth is not that river. The tiger already died in February water, with every son numbered. The White River has come for sails.
The epic battle: for the first time the West, Samhan, and the East meet in one mouth of water. Tang and Silla hold the banks; Baekje’s restoration and a Yamato expeditionary fleet come in on the tide — and discover, too late, that tide is not a friend you can hire.
## Four Banners
Count the banners before the water does. Tang comes by sea, twice. The Black Tortoise has held the old capital for two winters with a garrison too small to deserve the word. The emperor wrote that he could come home. He wrote back that he'd rather not. So in spring the emperor sends him seven thousand more. The Silla annals, which like round numbers, make it four hundred thousand.
Silla comes by land. King Munmu, in the third year of his reign, rides out of Surabol with Kim Yushin and twenty-eight generals behind him, thirty in another copy of the list. Yushin is sixty-eight and still sits a horse as if the horse had asked him to.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 6, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 3] The king led Kim Yushin and twenty-eight generals (one account says thirty), joined with them, and attacked Duryung-yunseong, Juryu and the other fortresses, and every one of them fell.
Baekje is what is left of it: a hill fortress called Juryu, a king who spent his boyhood in Yamato, and no Boksin. Two months ago the king had the general who crowned him beheaded, and the head is still in its jar.
Silla heard, and moved at once. A kingdom that executes its best general is a kingdom with its door open.
Upriver, King Pungjang still believes enough sails can restore a kingdom. For three summers the East has sent him ships. A thousand, if you trust the enemy's count. Forty-two thousand men. Takutsu is among the captains who still say Kudara. They come down on the eighth month's water, packed too tight to row. They are shouting for a victory the tide has already priced differently.
Takutsu brought Prince Pung home two years ago with five thousand men. Last winter he was the only one in the hall who told the new king not to move the court down to the plain, and he was right, and he was thanked for it the way men usually are.
On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, with the Silla army already on the road to Juryu, the king of Baekje announces that he will leave it.
pung: Yamato’s relief general, Lord Iohara, is crossing the sea with ten thousand men and more. / Generals, make ready for him. / I shall go down to Baekchon myself, and receive them there with a feast.
🙇: Majesty. And Juryu?
pung: Juryu has walls.
🙇: …It had a general, too.
## The Throat of the River
At Ungjin the allied generals argue about where to begin. Garim fortress sits where the road crosses the river, and most of the room wants it first.
liurengui: Garim is steep and strong. / Rush it and we bleed men. Sit under it and we bleed days. / Juryu is the nest. Pull the root, and the branches come down by themselves.
[QUOTE Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 84, Biography of Liu Rengui] Rengui said: “Garim is steep and strong. Attack it in haste and we lose soldiers; besiege it and the days drag on. Better to strike Juryu first. Juryu is the rebels’ nest, where the whole wicked crowd is gathered. To root out evil, go to the root. Take Juryu, and the other fortresses will come down of themselves.”
So the armies split. Most of the generals take the land road. The Black Tortoise takes the water: a hundred and seventy warships, heading for the river mouth. On his deck stands Buyeo Yung.
Euija’s eldest. He knelt at Sabi three summers ago, was taken to Chang’an with his father, and has come back in a Tang officer’s coat to fight his younger brother for the right to tell the survivors what happened to them. Nobody on the deck says this. Everybody on the deck knows it.
liurengui: Your brother’s banner will be on that fleet. / When it comes, can you look at it?
yung: I have looked at worse. / …I looked at my father.
The Black Tortoise has already learned the river's grammar. A narrow mouth. Sandbars that shift like lies. A current that punishes anyone who charges out of line. He anchors his hundred and seventy ships across the throat and waits. On the east bank, Kim Yushin's army keeps the shore from becoming a pier.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), eighth month] On the seventeenth, the enemy generals reached Juryu and surrounded the royal city. The generals of Great Tang led a hundred and seventy warships and drew them up in ranks on the Baekchon river.
## The Shore
On the bank the Baekje horsemen guard the landing. They are the last mounted men the restoration can field, drawn up in front of the beached hulls the way you stand in front of a door you cannot afford to lose. Silla’s cavalry comes at them first, out ahead of the Tang foot, because the king of Silla wants it written down later who went first.
munmu: Riders. With me. / When they write this down in Chang’an, I want Silla in the first line.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 7, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 11, his letter to Xue Rengui (671)] At that time the ship-borne troops of Wa came to help Baekje. A thousand Wa ships lay at Baeksa, and the picked horsemen of Baekje guarded the ships from the shore. The bold cavalry of Silla, as vanguard of the Han, broke the shore camp first; Juryu lost its nerve, and soon surrendered.
The shore camp goes in one charge. Yushin watches it from the ridge with the reins loose in one hand, which is how old generals watch something they no longer need to do themselves.
yushin: The unification of Samhan is not far off…
## The Twenty-Seventh Day
The first Yamato ships to arrive do not wait for the rest. They row straight at the Tang line on the evening water, and the Tang line does not move. It does not chase them, either. When the Yamato boats fall back, the hundred and seventy are exactly where they were that morning, in the same order, at anchor.
The Black Tortoise has seen men of Wa once before, in the emperor's city. They were envoys in court silk, and they bowed in all the right places. The court kept them in a guesthouse for two winters, so they couldn't carry home where the fleet was going. These are their cousins. They row standing up. They shout from too far away. They charge a hundred and seventy anchored hulls in boats built for rice. Nobody in his army has fought them before. He watches the first wave break on his line like a scholar reading a new script. He is looking for the grammar.
🙇: General— those are Wa? They’re… / …they’re rowing standing up.
liurengui: The last Wa I saw were bowing to the Son of Heaven. / Watch their oars, not their faces. The faces will stay brave all day.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), eighth month] On the twenty-seventh, the first of the Japanese fleet to arrive engaged the fleet of Great Tang. Japan had the worst of it and withdrew; Great Tang held its formation and kept its ground.
liurengui: Nobody chases. / Tomorrow they will all come back together, and they will come angry.
## The Twenty-Eighth Day
That night the Yamato captains and the king of Baekje hold council on a deck, and nobody looks at the sky. Abe no Hirafu does most of the talking. He is the rear general, a big man in a wolf-fur mantle who spent three summers chasing the Emishi along the cold northern coast, and he has the habit of men who have lived through bad water: he believes the sea gives way to whoever moves first.
abe: Yesterday was the vanguard. Today it’s all of us! / Ha— we go first. Whoever hits first, the other side gives way. That’s the sea. Every sea.
pung: …Yes. First. / Let them see the king’s ship at the front.
takutsu: The tide turns before noon. / …Nobody is listening. Good. Then I will go first too.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), eighth month] On the twenty-eighth, the Japanese generals and the king of Baekje, without observing the signs of the weather, said to one another: “If we strive to be first, they will surely draw back of themselves.” And they led the disordered ranks of the Japanese middle army forward against the firm formation of Great Tang.
The first charge hits a wall of hulls. The second finds the current turning against them — Tang waits for that turn the way a patient general waits for thirst. On the third and fourth, fire travels faster than orders: arrows wrapped for flame, ships brushed together until one burning deck becomes a neighbourhood. Four hundred eastern ships do not sink so much as spend themselves into light.
[QUOTE Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 84, Liu Renkui (劉仁軌) — Battle of the White River mouth (663) · cf. Samguk Sagi bk. 28, Baekje Annals: 煙炎灼天 海水爲丹] They burned four hundred of their ships; smoke and flame filled the sky, and the seawater was all red.
Then the wings close. The Tang ships that looked like a wall turn out to have been a door with two leaves, and they swing shut from left and right around the Yamato centre, so tight that the eastern ships cannot turn bow or stern, and men who cannot row and cannot climb go into the water in their armour.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), eighth month] Great Tang at once closed in on the ships from left and right and fought them in a ring. In a moment the imperial army was routed. Many leapt into the water and drowned. Neither bow nor stern could be turned about.
From the king’s ship Pung can see the far bank, and on it the Silla banners his father’s enemy raised and did not live to see here.
pung: Chunchu, you wretch… how dare you, to His Majesty…!
takutsu: Long live Kudara — Land of the Heavenly Deer….!
His ship is burning under him and he does not leave it. He fights on the deck until there is not enough deck left to fight on.
takutsu: Baekje must survive….
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), eighth month] Echi no Takutsu looked up to heaven and swore an oath, gnashed his teeth in fury, killed some dozens of men, and there fell in battle.
liurengui: Hold the line. Let the tide finish what the bowstrings began. / A river mouth is a judge. Today it judged the East.
At the back of the fleet Abe no Hirafu’s ships are still afloat. He has seen a lost tide before, on a colder sea. He turns them for home and hauls in every swimmer the hulls will carry, men in half their armour, men with no oars, and he does not laugh again until Tsukushi.
## Brothers
In the smoke a small boat gets away from the king’s ship with a handful of men in it and turns north. It is Pung. He leaves behind his fleet, his allies, his capital on the hill, and his sword.
[QUOTE Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 84, Biography of Liu Rengui] Yu Feng slipped free and fled; his treasured sword was taken.
They bring the sword to the Tang flagship. It is a Baekje ring-pommel blade with the ring worn smooth, nothing like a king’s, and the Black Tortoise hands it to the one man aboard who would know.
liurengui: Whose?
yung: …My brother’s. / Our father gave it to him the year they sent him east. He was seven.
liurengui: Shall I send boats after him?
yung: …North is Goguryeo. Let Goguryeo keep him. / He was always better at being sent away than I was.
## Juryu
Juryu holds ten more days without its king. On the seventh day of the ninth month it opens its gate. Pung’s younger brothers, the princes Chungseung and Chungji, walk out at the head of what is left: soldiers, women, the Yamato men who missed the boats, and an envoy from Tamla who came up the hill to bargain for an island and is now surrendering for it.
[QUOTE Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 84, Biography of Liu Rengui] The false princes Buyeo Chungseung, Chungji and the rest led out the men and women, together with the Wa host and the envoys of the land of Tamla, and all surrendered at once.
The people who are not surrendering go south, toward the port at Terye where the Yamato ships will take them off. On the road they say the thing to one another that the Yamato chronicle wrote down, because nobody was left in Baekje to write it.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), ninth month] Juryu has surrendered. Nothing more can be done. The name of Baekje ends today. The place of our ancestors’ graves — how can we ever go back to it?
One fortress doesn't hear it. Its commander shuts the gate and holds all autumn, and the siege goes home. In the end it falls to its own people's hands. Sangji and Sangya have changed sides. The Black Tortoise hands back their armour and points them up the slope.
sangji: The north wall is the low one. / I built it.
Ji Subsin leaves his wife and children inside and goes north to Goguryeo, which by now is where Baekje’s last kings go.
When the water cools to ordinary colour again, the restoration has no fleet worth the word. The Black Tortoise sits down with Kim Yushin. Neither of them believes a word the other says, and they get a great deal done — which is how alliances sound after four hundred ships have paid for the silence.
Two reapers failed to take Yeon Gesomun at the river. The ledger still has his name in it…!

=== EPISODE 84: Yeon Gesomun† (665)
## King Yumla
The Eternal General is dying.
gesomun: Do not… fight amongst yourselves…
namseng: Father. / You never kept a brother close. / One you sent to the far end of the southern border. The rest you cut down.
gesomun: …That is precisely why I am telling you.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Emperor Tenji, yr. 3 (664) — the dying words of the Goguryeo minister 蓋金] You brothers, be as close as fish and water. Do not quarrel over rank. If you do not heed this, you will surely be the laughingstock of your neighbours.
He expects one of them — Kangrim with his Question, or Haewonmek with his last words. He has been rehearsing a refusal.
gesomun: …Which of you failed me at the Snake River? / Come on. Ask. I am ready to say no again.
It is not either of them. Purple of sentence, not crow-dark of the fetch — Yumla himself stands in the room. The judge, not the clerks. A king for a king.
yumla: Yeon Gesomun. / My two best men could not bring you at the Snake River. / A man like you — only another king could carry you off. / Consider the courtesy returned.
gesomun: …Hah. / So the clerks failed, and the boss clocked in. / Fine. I always preferred dealing with the top.
yumla: The minutes will remember the joke. / Now — walk. Judgment keeps better hours than Supreme Commanders.
Yeon catches a vision of something at the very end. A young man, centuries off, saying Goryeo as if it had never gone.
He dies in his sleep, which is not how anyone expected it to go.
namseng: Well… even a man like that stands before Yumla in the end.
His eldest, Namseng, takes on the title of Supreme Commander. He is thirty-one, and it is very heavy.
Yeon Jungto, who raised the two younger boys at his own table, is at the southern border when the news comes. He writes to Namgun that night. The answer, when it comes, is in a secretary’s hand.
namgun: Gesomun… he really did have a gift, didn’t he.
namgun: If the old man were alive we would not be in this state.
— Yeon Gesomun —
Every single thing he said about his country was correct. The court was rotten. The tribute was a slow surrender. Taizong was coming whether or not they were polite about it. He was the only man in the room who could see it, and he was right, and being right is what destroyed him.
Because a man who is right and impatient does not build. He replaces. He killed the council and became the council. He killed the command and became the command. For twenty-two years Goguryeo did not need institutions, because it had him, and he was better than institutions — faster, braver, entirely unaccountable.
He outlasted the Second Emperor’s war and broke the White Tiger at the Snake River with his own hands, and every victory made the kingdom lean on him a little harder, until the whole weight of it rested on one man’s spine. A spine is a magnificent thing, but no one has ever built a house on one.
His last words were: do not fight one another. His eldest son answered that he had never kept a brother close: one sent to the border, the rest cut down. Both of them were telling the truth, and neither of them could hear it.
He held the north for a generation and left nothing behind him that could hold it for a year. Nine months after they buried him his sons were at war with each other. Twenty-six months after that his eldest was riding west to show the Third Emperor the road in.
“Do not fight amongst yourselves.” He had three sons. How long do you think that lasts?

=== EPISODE 85: Brothers’ Coup (666)
The Third Emperor invades Goguryeo again. Nobody is counting anymore. This time, he has a guide.
gaozong: I have already destroyed Baekje and removed your country’s worry; yet now Goryeo trusts in the ruggedness of its land, joins the Yemaek in wickedness, breaks the rite of serving a great state, and abandons the duty of living peaceably with its neighbours. I am sending soldiers to strike it — so return and tell your king to send out his army, and with us annihilate these failing barbarians.
## The Provinces
In the spring Namseng goes out to inspect the provinces, as a new Supreme Commander should, and leaves his two younger brothers to keep the capital.
Within a month there are men whispering in both directions. To Namgun and Namsan: your brother means to be rid of you when he comes back. To Namseng, at every post station: your brothers do not mean to let you back in.
namseng: Nonsense. They are my brothers. / …Send someone back anyway. Quietly. I want to know what they say at supper.
The man he sends is caught at the Pyongyang gate within the week. Namgun reads the orders found on him twice, and the second time he reads them as a confession.
namgun: He sends spies. To his own brothers. / Shut the gates! Tell the king the Supreme Commander has rebelled!
A messenger comes to the provincial camp with an urgent message. Namseng meets him in his quarters.
He rides back to his own capital and finds the gate shut. His brother comes up onto the wall.
namseng: Open the gate, Namgun. / You are speaking to the Supreme Commander.
namgun: Insolent— no. Then what would you have me do?
namseng: Traitor.
namgun: Traitor…?
namseng: How did Joseon fall? Through the betrayal of the king’s closest men. / They say the taller a man stands, the longer his shadow. / After Gesomun, there is no one in Goryeo who can reach even his shadow. / And his sons—
Namseng goes north to the old capital at Gungnae, and sends his son to Chang’an to ask the Third Emperor for an army.
## Defection of Yeon Namseng
Namseng rides west, across the river his father spent a lifetime holding.
namseng: Goryeo is nothing but swindlers and thieves — / a people beyond hope.
gaozong: …My father spoke of a boy he met at the Liao. / One who would not kneel.
namseng: Twenty years ago, Majesty. Your father and I, when he crossed the Liao. / I did not kneel then.
He is thirty-two years old, and his brother has taken his title, his city and his father’s seat, and this is the second time in his life he has been offered a house in Chang’an. Nobody flogs him for the answer this time.
namseng: Your Majesty will never conquer Samhan alone.
namseng: Emperor… Your Majesty… ten thousand years…!
Namseng is given a Tang title, and a vanguard command against his own country.
In the south their uncle Yeon Jungto, who raised two of them, waits to hear which nephew will send for him. Neither does. He takes twelve cities over to Silla, and the family is finished in three directions at once.
Namseng knows the road in. Now he rides it home, with the whole Tang army at his back…!

=== EPISODE 86: Pyongyang II (668)
## The Ninth Invasion
Three of the emperor's four beasts come for the city at once. The Blue Dragon leads. The Black Tortoise and the second White Tiger ride behind him.
xuerengui: Breaking a fortress… is like farming. / You know the season, you bring the water, you harvest. / Today is a harvest day.
There is no cruelty in him, which is precisely what makes him difficult: the men of Goguryeo can hate a butcher, but they cannot quite hate a farmer who treats siege-work as weather.
namsan: Brother…
namseng: At last… I set foot on Pyongyang’s ground—
namgun: Goguryeo… never dies….!
## Betrayal from Inside
When the Tang ring closes, Namgun needs one man nobody can buy. He picks a monk. Shinsung has kept a small temple at the foot of the hill for twenty-five years. He has never asked anyone for anything.
namgun: You have no clan, no faction, no sons. / You’re the only man in this city I can’t imagine selling it.
shinsung: Then I shall try to be worthy of your imagination, Mangniji.
For five days a novice walks out of the lesser house before dawn with an alms bowl and comes back with it empty, and nobody thinks to ask why a monk’s bowl should come back empty from the direction of the Tang lines. On the fifth night the bell that has sat on the floor of the lesser house since the year the Daoists came is struck once.
Yeon once tried to starve the temples with the emperor's Daoists. The monks have waited a generation. Shinsung doesn't make a speech about doctrine. He opens a gate. Betrayal is a liturgy too. It's just performed from the inside.
The monk Shinsung and general Yomyo open the gates of the Fortress, letting the Tang army inside.
## Last Words
Namgun is thirty-one. He leads the last stand against the Blue Dragon himself.
namgun: Silla’s sacred blood — rot! / Goguryeo will take the final victory! / You may rule this soil — our name will have the last word!
The wall is already lost. He knows it. He says it anyway, to the men who can still hear, and to a bloodline across the river he can't see. Somebody, centuries from now, will be listening.
namgun: Goguryeo… never dies….!
When the gate towers burn, Namgun stabs himself in his own hall. He does it badly, the first thing he has done badly in the whole war, and the Tang surgeons save him so that he can be sent alive to the farthest edge of the empire.
When the city falls, the empire doesn't send a stranger to hold it. It sends Xue Rengui. The white coat becomes a banner over a broken capital. He governs well enough that even the conquered prefer him to chaos.
xuerengui: I… did not wish to be your enemy. / But I could not leave His Majesty’s east empty-handed.
The minutes are shorter than the kingdom. Goguryeo had stood seven hundred years. The king was taken to Chang’an. The record, for its part, writes only the month and the surrender.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 22, Goguryeo Annals — King Bojang, yr. 27 (668), 9th month; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 328 · cf. Zizhi Tongjian Tang Zongzhang 1] In the ninth month they took Pyongyang Fortress; King Bojang of Goguryeo surrendered.
Before the captives are shown to the living emperor, the Blue Dragon takes them up the mountain to show them to the dead one. The king of Goguryeo is made to bow at Zhaoling, in front of the door the Second Emperor said his horses would guard. The six stone horses stand in their row. The purple one is nearest the door.
The seventeen grades stop at one another. In the tenth month, after the city is open, King Munmu cuts a rank the grades did not have, and gives it to the man who has been Marshal since the yard.
munmu: Marshal.
yushin: Majesty.
munmu: You have been Marshal since before I could hold a bow. / The yard still says it. / The seventeen grades do not reach you anymore.
yushin: The word is enough. / I know what I am.
munmu: There was already a grade above the seventeen. / I had them cut one above that. / 태대각간. Supreme General.
yushin: A new name for an old man.
munmu: It is the name of the man who opened this city. / Wear it. / You may keep Marshal for the boys on the yard.
yushin: …As you command.
The story isn’t over yet. The Third Emperor still controls large swaths of Samhan. The final war begins…!
